# How to Cut a Round Cake Neatly (and Get More Slices)
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/how-to-cut-a-round-cake/

Use a long, thin knife, dip it in hot water and wipe it dry before every cut, and cut straight down without sawing. For a cake bigger than 20 cm, don't cut wedges from the centre; cut a ring about 5 cm in from the edge, slice that ring into pieces, then repeat with the inner circle. You'll get neater slices and far more of them. I've watched beautiful cakes destroyed in thirty seconds by a blunt kitchen knife and good intentions. It's always someone's uncle, and he always says he knows what he's doing. Here's what actually works. What you need - A long, thin, sharp knife. A bread knife is not ideal for cream cakes; it tears. A long chef's knife or a cake knife is better. - A tall jug of hot water. - A clean kitchen towel. - A cake server or a flat spatula. - Plates within reach, not across the room. Chill it first (a little) A cake straight from a warm room is soft and smears. A cake straight from the fridge is firm but the flavour is muted. The sweet spot is about 15 to 20 minutes out of the fridge for cream and buttercream cakes: firm enough to cut cleanly, soft enough to taste. The warm-blade trick Dip the knife in hot water for a few seconds, wipe it dry with the towel, and cut. The warm blade slides through frosting instead of dragging it. Do this before every single cut. Yes, every one. It's the single biggest difference between neat slices and a smeared mess. Cut straight down in one smooth motion, pressing gently, then pull the knife out towards you rather than lifting it back up through the slice. Small cakes (up to about 20 cm): wedges For a 500 g to 1 kg round cake, wedges are fine. 1. Cut the cake in half. 2. Cut each half in half again, so you have quarters. 3. Cut each quarter into two or three wedges, depending on how many you need. A 1 kg round cut this way gives 8 to 12 slices. Bigger cakes: the ring method Wedges from a big cake are huge at the outside and nearly nothing at the tip. The ring method fixes that. 1. Cut a circle about 5 cm in from the outer edge, all the way around. 2. Cut that outer ring into slices about 2.5 to 3 cm wide. 3. Cut another circle 5 cm further in. 4. Slice that ring the same way. 5. Keep going until the small centre is left, then cut it into wedges. A 2 kg cake cut with this method easily serves 25 neat pieces. Tiered cakes 1. Remove the top tier first (and any toppers, dowels and supports, which are not edible). 2. Cut the bottom tier with the ring method. 3. Cut the top tier separately, or keep it for the family. Some families keep the top tier of a wedding or anniversary cake for later. If you plan to, tell your baker, and we'll tell you how long that particular cake will keep. Fondant cakes Fondant resists the knife. Score through the fondant layer first with the tip of a warm knife, then cut down through the cake. Many guests will peel the fondant off anyway, so don't worry if the sides aren't perfect. Cheesecakes and brownies Cheesecakes love the warm-blade trick more than anything else. Brownies cut best when they're cool and slightly firm; cutting warm brownies tastes wonderful and looks terrible. Serving Lay each slice on its side on the plate, not upright, so it doesn't topple. And give the birthday person the first slice, the one with their name on it. It's tradition for a reason. If you'd like a cake that's easier to cut, ask for a buttercream or ganache finish over fresh cream; they hold clean edges better. More on that in our cakes page. How do you cut a cake without it crumbling? Chill the cake for a short while, use a long thin knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry before each cut, and cut straight down without sawing. How many slices do you get from a 1 kg cake? A 1 kg round cake gives 8 to 12 party slices when cut into wedges, and a few more with the ring method. What's the best way to cut a big round cake? Cut a circle about 5 cm in from the edge, slice that ring into even pieces, then repeat with the next circle in. It gives neater, more even slices than cutting wedges from the centre.

---

# What Replaces Eggs in an Eggless Cake, and Why It's Still Soft
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/what-replaces-eggs-in-eggless-cake/

In an eggless cake, curd (yogurt), milk, condensed milk, oil or butter, and a balanced mix of baking powder and baking soda take over the jobs eggs normally do: binding, rising, moisture and richness. Done carefully, an eggless sponge is just as soft as one with eggs. Done carelessly, it's dense and gummy, which is why eggless cakes got a bad name. I bake a lot of eggless cakes. In Chennai, for many families, an eggless cake is simply what a cake is. So I've spent a long time learning how to make them stand on their own. What eggs actually do To replace something properly you need to know what it was doing. In a cake, eggs do four things. They bind. Egg proteins set as they heat, holding the crumb together so the cake slices instead of falling apart. They help it rise. Beaten eggs trap air, and that air expands in the oven. Eggs also turn to steam, which lifts the cake. They add moisture and fat. The yolk especially brings richness and a tender texture. They emulsify. Yolks help fat and water mix smoothly, giving a fine, even crumb. An eggless cake has to cover all four. What does the work instead Curd (yogurt). My favourite. It adds moisture and a gentle tang, and its acidity reacts with baking soda to produce lift. Cakes made with curd have a soft, slightly springy crumb, almost velvety. It's also an ingredient every Chennai kitchen already has. Milk and a little vinegar or lemon. The same idea as buttermilk. The acid helps the raising agents and keeps the cake tender. Condensed milk. Adds richness, sweetness and binding. Wonderful in vanilla and butterscotch cakes, but it's sweet, so the sugar is reduced to balance it. Oil or butter. Oil keeps an eggless cake moist for longer, which is why many eggless chocolate cakes use it. Butter gives better flavour. I often use both. Baking powder and baking soda, measured carefully. Too little and the cake is heavy. Too much and it rises fast, collapses, and tastes faintly soapy. This is where most bad eggless cakes go wrong. Mashed banana, applesauce, flaxseed. Useful in some bakes, especially wholesome ones like banana bread, but they bring their own flavour and texture, so I use them selectively. Why some eggless cakes turn out dense If you've had a heavy eggless cake, it was probably one of these: - Overmixing. Without eggs, gluten develops more easily. Mix too long and the cake turns chewy. - Too much raising agent, which makes it rise and sink. - The wrong flour balance. Eggless sponges are more delicate; they need a lighter hand. - Baking too hot, which sets the outside before the inside rises. - A recipe that just "took the eggs out" of an egg cake without rebalancing everything else. Does it taste different? Slightly, and often in a good way. Curd-based eggless sponges have a faint tang that's lovely with fruit and cream. Chocolate eggless cakes are very hard to tell apart from egg-based ones; the cocoa takes centre stage. Where you'll notice the difference most is in very light, airy sponges like a classic chiffon, which rely heavily on whipped egg. For those, I adjust the recipe rather than pretend. Eggless doesn't mean vegan, or allergy-safe Two things worth knowing. Eggless bakes usually contain milk, butter and curd, so they aren't vegan. And most home kitchens, including mine, also bake with eggs. I use separate bowls and wash everything carefully between batches, but if someone has a severe egg allergy, please tell me before ordering so we can talk about it properly. There's more on this in our guide to ordering an eggless birthday cake. What is used instead of eggs in eggless cakes? Eggless cakes usually use curd (yogurt), milk with a little vinegar or lemon, condensed milk, oil or butter, and a careful balance of baking powder and baking soda to replace what eggs do. Are eggless cakes as soft as normal cakes? Yes, when made well. Curd and milk give a tender, moist crumb, and many people can't tell a good eggless cake from one made with eggs. Is eggless cake healthier than egg cake? Not necessarily. Eggless cakes contain similar amounts of sugar and fat. They're chosen for dietary, religious or allergy reasons rather than health.

---

# Ordering an Eggless Birthday Cake in Chennai: Questions to Ask First
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/eggless-birthday-cake-chennai/

Before you order an eggless birthday cake, ask four things: is the whole cake eggless (sponge, filling and frosting), what replaces the egg, is it baked in a kitchen that also uses eggs, and are the decorations eggless too. Those answers matter most for families who don't eat eggs for religious reasons, and for anyone with an allergy. In Chennai, "Is it eggless?" might be the most common question a baker hears. Grandparents who have never eaten egg. Friends who keep fasting days. Jain and many Hindu families. Children with egg allergies. Offices that simply want one cake everyone can share. If you're one of them, here's what's worth checking. Our eggless menu answers most of these for The Bake Basket. 1. Is every part of the cake eggless? A cake is more than the sponge. Some frostings, especially certain buttercreams and meringue-based ones, use egg whites. Some fillings, such as custards and curds, use yolks. Macarons on top contain egg white. Store-bought sprinkles and decorations sometimes contain egg-based glazes. Ask: "Is the sponge, filling, frosting and decoration all eggless?" A good baker will answer without hesitation. 2. What's used instead? You don't need a chemistry lecture, but it's reasonable to know. Most good eggless cakes use curd, milk, condensed milk, oil or butter and raising agents. Some bakeries use commercial egg replacer powders, which are fine, but you may want to know. There's a full explanation in what replaces eggs in an eggless cake. 3. Does the kitchen also use eggs? Almost every home bakery does. That's not a problem for most eggless customers; it's like a family kitchen where some people eat eggs and others don't. But for strict religious observance or a serious allergy, it matters. Ask: "Do you use separate utensils for eggless orders? How do you prevent cross-contact?" An honest baker will tell you what they do and what they can't guarantee. Be wary of anyone who says "100% egg-free" while also selling egg puffs. 4. Is it a Jain-friendly cake? Eggless is only part of it. Strict Jain diets also avoid root vegetables, honey, certain additives and, for some families, gelatin and some colours or flavourings. Many cake ingredients are fine, but things like gelatin in mousse, some flavour extracts, or honey in a glaze may not be. Ask the baker to walk you through every ingredient. If they don't know what's in their frosting colour or sprinkles, choose a simpler design with fewer bought decorations. 5. What about vegan? Eggless and vegan aren't the same. Most eggless cakes contain milk, butter, cream and curd. A vegan cake uses plant milks and fats instead. If someone is vegan or dairy-allergic, say so clearly. 6. Does every flavour come eggless? Most do. Chocolate truffle, butterscotch, pineapple, black forest, red velvet, rasmalai and fruit cakes all adapt well. The flavours that are hardest are the ones built around eggs themselves, like custard-based fillings or a very light chiffon. A good baker will steer you towards what works best. 7. Is there a price difference? Some bakers charge a little extra for eggless because the recipe takes different ingredients and more care. Others don't. Ask up front so there are no surprises. Should the whole party cake just be eggless? Often, yes. If a third of your guests are eggless, a single eggless cake means nobody gets "the other cake" and the cutting ceremony stays simple. Most people won't notice the difference. Offices in particular tend to go fully eggless for this reason. A small note on labels The green dot on packaged food in India marks it as vegetarian, which under FSSAI rules can include milk products but not eggs. Home bakers don't always use packaged-food labels, so the conversation with your baker is your real guarantee. Can I get an eggless birthday cake in Chennai? Yes. Many home bakers in Chennai, including The Bake Basket, make most birthday cake flavours eggless. Ask whether the sponge, frosting and decorations are all eggless when you order. Is an eggless cake suitable for Jains? An eggless cake can be suitable, but strict Jain diets avoid other ingredients too, such as honey, gelatin and some additives. Ask your baker to go through every ingredient with you. Do eggless cakes cost more? Some bakers charge slightly more for eggless cakes and some don't. Ask about pricing when you order.

---

# Is Ragi Cake Gluten-Free? What Millet Bakes Really Are
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/is-ragi-cake-gluten-free/

Ragi (finger millet) is naturally gluten-free. Most ragi cakes are not. To get a soft, cake-like texture, the majority of ragi recipes mix ragi flour with wheat flour or maida, sometimes as much as half and half. A ragi cake is gluten-free only if it's made with no wheat at all and in conditions that avoid cross-contact, so if gluten matters to you, ask. That's the headline. The rest of this post is about why ragi is still worth eating in a cake, and how to choose millet bakes with your eyes open. If you're looking to order, our healthy bakes page lists what we make. What ragi is Ragi, kezhvaragu in Tamil, finger millet in English, is one of the oldest grains in South Indian kitchens. Ragi koozh in summer, ragi kali in villages, ragi dosai, ragi puttu. Many of our grandparents ate it daily. Nutritionally, it's notable for its calcium content, which is high for a grain, and it's a good source of dietary fibre. It has a deep, earthy, slightly nutty taste and a reddish-brown colour that looks almost like cocoa. Why bakers mix it with wheat Gluten is the protein network in wheat that gives bread its chew and cake its structure. Ragi has none. On its own, ragi flour makes a cake that's tender, crumbly and dense, a bit like a very soft fudge. That's wonderful in a brownie, which is supposed to be dense. It's harder in a light birthday sponge. So most recipes add some wheat flour, whole-wheat atta or maida to help it hold together and rise. The result tastes of ragi, has more fibre than a plain cake, and is no longer gluten-free. Where ragi shines Brownies. This is where ragi is at its best. Its natural density and earthy flavour sit beautifully with dark chocolate, and children usually can't tell. A ragi brownie can be made with no wheat at all. Cookies. Ragi cookies with jaggery and a little ghee are crisp, nutty and very moreish. Banana bread and loaf cakes. Ragi with banana and whole wheat makes a moist, filling tea-time cake. Puttu and steamed foods. Ragi puttu needs no baking at all, and is naturally gluten-free. What "ragi cake" can mean on a menu Label What it might contain ------ Ragi cake Usually ragi plus wheat or maida Ragi and whole-wheat cake Ragi plus atta, no maida 100% ragi cake Ragi as the only flour; check binders and cross-contact Gluten-free ragi cake Should contain no wheat, barley or rye; ask about the kitchen Ragi brownie Often 100% ragi, sometimes mixed None of these are wrong. They're just different. What matters is that the label tells you which one you're getting. Is a ragi cake healthier? Healthier than a plain maida cake, in some ways. More fibre, more minerals, often more filling. But it's still cake. It still has sugar (or jaggery, which is also sugar; more on that in jaggery vs sugar), still has fat, and still deserves to be a treat rather than breakfast. Where millet bakes really help is at a family table where different people have different needs. Appa watching his sugar, a teenager avoiding maida, a child who just likes chocolate. A ragi brownie can make all three happy. If someone has coeliac disease Coeliac disease is a medical condition where even small amounts of gluten cause harm. If someone in your family has it, ask your baker very specific questions: is the bake made with no wheat, barley or rye at all? Are oats used, and are they certified gluten-free? Are separate utensils and surfaces used? Is the kitchen also baking with wheat that day? Most home kitchens, The Bake Basket's included, also use wheat flour. Priya will always tell you honestly what she can and can't promise. Is ragi gluten-free? Yes, ragi (finger millet) is naturally gluten-free. But most ragi cakes are mixed with wheat flour for texture, so they are not gluten-free unless made specifically without wheat. Is ragi cake good for health? Ragi cake usually has more fibre and minerals than a plain maida cake and can be more filling, but it still contains sugar and fat, so it's best enjoyed as a treat. Can people with gluten intolerance eat ragi brownies? Only if the brownies are made with no wheat flour and the baker takes care to avoid cross-contact. Ask the baker exactly how they're made.

# Jaggery vs Sugar in Cakes: Is a Jaggery Cake Healthier?
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/jaggery-vs-sugar-in-cakes/

A jaggery cake is a better-quality treat, not a low-sugar one. Jaggery is less refined than white sugar and keeps small amounts of minerals such as iron and potassium, and it gives cakes a lovely caramel depth. But it is still mostly sugar, with a similar calorie count, and it raises blood glucose in much the same way. Choose jaggery for flavour and for less processing. Don't choose it as diabetic food. That isn't what everyone wants to hear, so let me explain properly, and then explain why Priya still loves baking with it. You'll find our jaggery bakes on the healthy bakes page. What jaggery is Jaggery (vellam in Tamil, sharkara in Malayalam) is made by boiling sugarcane juice, or the sap of palms, until it thickens and sets. Because it isn't refined the way white sugar is, some of the molasses and minerals stay in. That's what gives it its colour, its smell and its flavour. Palm jaggery (karupatti) comes from palm sap and has a smokier, deeper taste. Nattu sakkarai, often sold as country sugar, is a granulated, less refined cane sugar that behaves a little more like brown sugar in baking. What it adds Flavour. This is the real reason to bake with it. Jaggery brings caramel, toffee and a faint smokiness. In a banana loaf, a date cake or a ragi brownie, it tastes like it belongs. Small amounts of minerals. Jaggery contains some iron, potassium and magnesium that refined sugar loses. The amounts in a slice of cake are small, but it's something. Less processing. For many families, choosing ingredients closer to how they come from the farm matters, and jaggery fits that. What it doesn't change Calories. Gram for gram, jaggery has roughly the same calories as white sugar. Blood sugar. Jaggery is mainly sucrose, the same sugar as white sugar, with some glucose and fructose. Its effect on blood glucose is broadly similar. There's no strong evidence that it's safe for people with diabetes in amounts where white sugar wouldn't be. The fact that it's a treat. A jaggery cake is still cake. How it behaves in baking Jaggery is a little trickier than sugar. It's moist and variable, so batches differ in sweetness and colour. It can make cakes denser and darker. It caramelises faster, so cakes brown sooner. And it pairs better with some flavours than others. Brilliant with: banana, dates, ragi, wheat, coconut, cardamom, dry ginger, chocolate, coffee, walnuts. Less good with: delicate vanilla sponges, light fruit cakes, anything meant to be pale and airy. Who should be careful Anyone with diabetes, prediabetes or insulin resistance should treat a jaggery cake like any other cake: a small piece, ideally after a meal, and in line with their doctor's advice. If that's the situation in your family, read our post on choosing a cake when someone has diabetes. And for babies under one, the general advice is to avoid added sugars of any kind, jaggery included. So why bake with it at all? Because it tastes like home. Because it makes a better cake in the right recipe. And because for a family trying to eat a little more simply, swapping refined sugar for jaggery in an occasional treat is a reasonable, honest step, as long as no one is told it's a health food. That's how The Bake Basket labels its jaggery bakes: no refined sugar. Never sugar-free, because they aren't. Is jaggery cake good for health? Jaggery cake is less processed than a white-sugar cake and contains small amounts of minerals, but it has similar calories and still raises blood sugar. It's a better treat, not a health food. Is jaggery better than sugar for diabetics? No. Jaggery is mostly sucrose and affects blood glucose much like white sugar. People with diabetes should limit it in the same way and follow medical advice. Does jaggery cake taste different? Yes. It's darker and has a caramel, toffee-like flavour. It suits banana, date, ragi, coconut and chocolate cakes especially well.

---

# Choosing a Cake When Someone in the Family Has Diabetes
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/cake-for-diabetic-family-member/

There's no cake that's simply "safe" for diabetics, but there are much better choices. Pick a smaller cake made with less sugar, more fibre (whole wheat, millets, nuts) and a lighter frosting; serve a thin slice after a meal rather than on its own; and ask your baker plainly what's in it. Above all, follow the advice your family member's doctor has given, because diabetes is managed differently for different people. I'm not a doctor, and this isn't medical advice. It's what we've learned from many families who've asked us the same question: how do we celebrate Appa's 70th without him sitting out the cake? First, the words on the menu "Sugar-free" can mean many things. Sometimes it means a sugar substitute like a sugar alcohol or stevia blend has been used instead of sugar. Those can help, but the cake still contains flour, which becomes glucose in the body, and some substitutes affect blood sugar more than others. "No added sugar" or "no refined sugar" often means the cake is sweetened with jaggery, dates, honey or fruit. These are still sugars. "Reduced sugar" means less sugar than the usual recipe. Less, not none. We go through all three in detail in sugar-free, no added sugar, reduced sugar. What tends to be a better choice Smaller, richer cakes. A thin slice of something satisfying beats a big slice of something light. A dense ragi brownie or a nutty date and walnut loaf is eaten slowly. More fibre. Whole wheat, ragi, oats and nuts slow down how quickly the cake is digested compared with a pure maida sponge. Less frosting. The frosting is often the most sugar-dense part. A simple cake with a thin layer, or a loaf cake with no frosting, is a better pick than a cream-loaded celebration cake. Reduced sugar overall. Ask the baker to cut sugar in the sponge, the syrup and the frosting. Fresh fruit on top instead of syrupy fillings. What tends to be a worse choice - Large slices of soft maida sponge with lots of cream or buttercream - Syrup-soaked cakes like rasmalai and tres leches style cakes - Fondant, which is almost pure sugar - Cakes eaten on an empty stomach, mid-afternoon - Anything labelled "diabetic-friendly" without telling you exactly what's in it Practical ideas for the day Two cakes. A smaller, regular celebration cake for the cutting and photos, plus a reduced-sugar millet bake or loaf for the people watching sugar. Nobody feels singled out. A small cake for the birthday person. If it's Appa's birthday, give him his own bento-sized reduced-sugar cake with his name on it. It's his moment, not a compromise. Cut thinly. Offer a sliver. Many people just want the taste and the ritual. Time it after the meal. Cake after a balanced dinner affects blood sugar less dramatically than cake on its own. Talk to the doctor. Some people with well-managed diabetes can enjoy a small piece of regular cake; others are advised strictly. Their own doctor knows. What to ask your baker 1. What sweetener is in the sponge, the filling and the frosting? 2. How much less sugar than your normal recipe? 3. What flour is used? 4. Can the frosting be lighter, or can we skip it? 5. If you use a sugar substitute, which one? An honest baker will answer clearly, and won't promise you anything they can't stand behind. At The Bake Basket, the healthy bakes are labelled with exactly what's in them, and nothing is ever called diabetic-safe. Can diabetics eat birthday cake? Many people with diabetes can enjoy a small portion of cake occasionally, especially after a meal, but it depends on their individual condition and their doctor's advice. Choose smaller portions, less frosting and reduced-sugar, higher-fibre recipes. Is sugar-free cake safe for diabetics? Not automatically. Sugar-free cakes still contain flour, which raises blood glucose, and some sweeteners affect blood sugar too. Treat sugar-free cake as a better option, not a free one. What is the best cake for a diabetic person? A small portion of a reduced-sugar cake made with whole grains, millets or nuts, with little or no frosting, is usually a better choice than a regular cream cake.

---

# Sugar-Free, No Added Sugar, Reduced Sugar: What the Labels Mean
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/sugar-free-vs-no-added-sugar/

"Sugar-free" should mean the product has almost no sugar at all, usually because a substitute is used. "No added sugar" means no sugar was added beyond what's naturally in the ingredients, such as fruit or milk. "No refined sugar" means white sugar wasn't used, though jaggery, honey or dates might have been. "Reduced sugar" means less than the usual recipe. Four labels, four different things. On packaged foods in India, terms like "sugar-free" and "low sugar" are defined in FSSAI's labelling and claims regulations, with specific limits. Home bakers selling unpackaged cakes don't always follow that framework strictly, and the words get used loosely. So it's worth knowing what to ask. Our healthy bakes are labelled with the plainest words we could find. Sugar-free On a packaged product, "sugar-free" has a strict regulatory meaning: very little sugar per serving. In a bakery, it usually means sugar has been replaced with a substitute: stevia, sucralose, erythritol, maltitol or a blend. What to know: - The cake still contains flour, which your body turns into glucose. - Some substitutes, like maltitol, still raise blood sugar somewhat and can upset the stomach in larger amounts. - Others, like stevia and erythritol, have little effect on blood sugar but can taste different, sometimes with a slight cooling or bitter note. Ask: "Which sweetener?" No added sugar Nothing sweet was added, but the ingredients may be naturally sweet. A banana cake with no added sugar gets its sweetness from very ripe bananas. A date cake gets it from dates. What to know: fruit sugar is still sugar. A cake sweetened entirely with dates can be just as sweet, and contain nearly as much sugar, as one made with white sugar. The difference is that fruit brings fibre and other nutrients with it. No refined sugar This is the label The Bake Basket uses most for its wholesome bakes. It means no white sugar or refined sweeteners, but the cake is sweetened with jaggery, palm jaggery, coconut sugar, honey or dates. What to know: these are all sugars. They're less processed and taste more interesting, but they affect your body in broadly similar ways. More on this in jaggery vs sugar in cakes. Reduced sugar or less sugar The recipe uses less sugar than the baker's standard version, often by a quarter to a third. It's a simple, honest option that many families like because the cake still tastes like the cake they know, just less sweet. What to know: ask "reduced by how much?" A good baker will know. A side-by-side Label Sugar added? Natural sugars? Typical sweetener Good for --------------- Sugar-free No (substitute used) Possibly, from flour and dairy Stevia, erythritol, sucralose, maltitol People strictly limiting sugar, with care No added sugar No Yes Ripe fruit, dates Families who want natural sweetness No refined sugar Yes, unrefined Yes Jaggery, honey, dates, coconut sugar Less processed treats with more flavour Reduced sugar Yes, less Yes White sugar, in smaller amounts The familiar cake, gentler Why bakers blur these Mostly because "sugar-free" sells. It's an attractive phrase, and it's easy to stretch. But families who are managing a parent's diabetes, or cutting down for their own health, deserve to know exactly what they're eating. Misleading them, even with good intentions, can do harm. So the rule in Priya's kitchen is simple. If it has jaggery, the label says jaggery. If it has less sugar, it says how much less. "Sugar-free" is never used unless it truly is. What is the difference between sugar-free and no added sugar? Sugar-free means the product contains almost no sugar, usually because a sugar substitute was used. No added sugar means no sugar was added, but natural sugars from fruit, milk or dates are still present. Does no refined sugar mean healthy? No refined sugar means white sugar wasn't used, but the cake is usually sweetened with jaggery, honey or dates, which are still sugars. It's less processed, not sugar-free. What does reduced sugar mean in a cake? Reduced sugar means the cake has less sugar than the baker's standard recipe, often a quarter to a third less. Ask the baker for the exact reduction.

# Lunchbox Bakes Chennai Kids Will Actually Eat
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/healthy-lunchbox-bakes-for-kids/

The lunchbox bakes that come home empty are small, not too sweet, sturdy enough to survive a hot classroom, and familiar enough that a child recognises them as a treat. Think millet banana muffins, veggie and cheese muffins, whole-wheat banana bread, ragi cookies and plain butter-free oat bars. Keep anything with cream, chocolate coating or nuts out of the school box. Every parent in Chennai knows the 4 pm moment: the lunchbox opens, and either it's empty, or the same thing you packed this morning stares back at you, slightly warmer. This post is about the first outcome. Our healthy bakes include the lunchbox range. What makes a good lunchbox bake It survives the heat. School bags sit in warm classrooms for five hours. Anything with cream, custard or a chocolate coating will melt, smear or spoil. Muffins, loaf cakes, cookies and dense bars are reliable. It's small. A full slice of cake feels like too much in a short break. Mini muffins, half slices and two-bite cookies get finished. It isn't too sweet. A treat that's very sweet usually means a sugar crash by the last period. Lightly sweetened bakes with fruit, jaggery or a little honey are a better fit, and they still taste like a treat. It's familiar. Children are suspicious of new food, especially in front of friends. Banana bread looks like cake. A muffin looks like a cupcake. That matters more than what's inside. It's school-safe. Many Chennai schools ask for nut-free lunchboxes because of allergies. Check your school's rules and stick to them. Ideas that work Millet banana muffins. Ripe banana, ragi or a millet mix with whole wheat, a little jaggery. Soft, moist, naturally sweet. Veggie and cheese muffins. Grated carrot, corn, a little capsicum, cheese, whole-wheat flour. Savoury, filling, and a sneaky way to add vegetables. Whole-wheat banana bread. Slice thick, wrap in butter paper, and it travels beautifully. Ragi cookies. Crisp, nutty, made with jaggery. Pack two, not five. Oat and date bars. Chewy, filling and naturally sweet. Make sure they're nut-free for school. Mini savoury buns. Soft whole-wheat buns with a mild paneer or vegetable filling. Carrot and coconut cake. Moist, mildly spiced, and tastes like something a grandmother would make. What to avoid - Cream or buttercream anything - Chocolate-coated or chocolate-dipped bakes (they melt) - Nuts, if the school is nut-free - Very crumbly bakes, which turn to dust in a lunchbox - Anything that needs a fork Pairing ideas A bake is part of the box, not the whole box. A few combinations that work well: - Mini idli with podi, plus a millet muffin - Chapati roll, cucumber slices, plus a ragi cookie - Vegetable sandwich, apple slices, plus a square of banana bread - Curd rice (in a separate container), plus an oat bar for the short break Storage tips for parents Muffins and banana bread keep two to three days in an airtight box at room temperature in cool weather. In Chennai summers, keep them in the fridge and pack them in the morning; they'll come to room temperature by break time. Most muffins also freeze well: freeze individually, take one out the night before. If you'd rather not bake at 6 am on a school day, ask us about lunchbox bakes. What are healthy snacks for kids' school lunchboxes? Small, lightly sweetened bakes like millet banana muffins, veggie muffins, whole-wheat banana bread, ragi cookies and nut-free oat bars work well, paired with fruit or a savoury item. How do I keep lunchbox snacks fresh in hot weather? Choose sturdy bakes without cream or chocolate coatings, store them in the fridge overnight, and pack them in the morning in an airtight box. Are millet muffins good for kids? Millet muffins usually have more fibre and minerals than plain maida muffins and are more filling, which makes them a good lunchbox treat, though they still contain some sugar.

# Sourdough vs Regular Bread: Is Sourdough Really Better for You?
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/sourdough-vs-regular-bread/

Real sourdough is leavened with a wild starter of flour and water instead of packaged yeast, and fermented slowly, often overnight. That long fermentation gives it a crisp crust, a chewy, open crumb and a gentle tang. Research suggests the fermentation can make sourdough easier for some people to digest and may give it a gentler effect on blood sugar than many white breads. It's a better everyday bread. It is not a health food, and it is not gluten-free. I have a jar on my counter that I feed every day, like a slightly needy pet. That's my starter, and it's the whole difference between sourdough and the soft loaf in a plastic bag. You can see what we bake on our breads page. What sourdough actually is Most bread is made with commercial yeast, a single, fast-working strain that makes dough rise in an hour or two. Sourdough uses a "starter" instead: flour and water left to ferment until wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria settle in and multiply. Feed it regularly and it becomes a living culture. When it's mixed into dough, the yeasts produce gas, which makes the bread rise, slowly. The bacteria produce lactic and acetic acids, which give the tang. A sourdough loaf might take 12 to 36 hours from mixing to baking. What that slow fermentation changes Flavour. Long fermentation develops complex, slightly sour, almost nutty flavours that fast bread can't have. Texture. A thick, crackling crust and a chewy, glossy, open crumb with irregular holes. Keeping. The acidity helps sourdough stay fresh longer than yeasted bread without preservatives. Mine is still good on day three. Digestion, possibly. During long fermentation, some of the carbohydrates known as FODMAPs break down, and the bacteria partly break down some of the gluten proteins. Some people who find regular bread uncomfortable find sourdough easier. That's not the same as being safe for coeliac disease; it isn't. Blood sugar, possibly. Several studies have found that sourdough bread produces a lower blood sugar response than comparable yeasted white bread, likely because of the acids. The effect varies with the flour, and a whole-grain loaf of any kind generally does better than white. What it doesn't change Sourdough made from white flour is still mostly refined carbohydrate. It has similar calories to regular bread. And it still contains gluten, even if some is broken down. So: a better bread, not a magic one. How to tell real sourdough from imitation A lot of bread sold as sourdough in India is ordinary yeasted bread with a sour flavouring or a little starter added for show. Here's how to tell: - Ingredients. Real sourdough needs only flour, water and salt. If the label lists yeast, or vinegar, it's a shortcut. - Price and availability. A real sourdough takes a day or more and some skill. Very cheap sourdough available everywhere at any time is suspicious. - Crumb. Real sourdough has an irregular, open crumb and a shine on the inside. A tight, even, fluffy crumb suggests a fast yeasted dough. - Crust. Thick, dark, crackling, often with an "ear" where it was scored. - Taste. A gentle tang that grows as you chew. Not a sharp vinegar note. - Ask. "How old is your starter, and how long is the fermentation?" A real sourdough baker will happily tell you about both. How to eat it Thick slices, toasted, with butter. With a good curry, like a Kerala stew. As a sandwich bread for something substantial. Torn into a salad. Don't keep it in the fridge; it goes stale fast there. Wrap it in a cloth or bag at room temperature, and freeze slices you won't eat in two or three days. Is sourdough bread healthier than regular bread? Sourdough's long fermentation may make it easier to digest for some people and can give it a gentler blood sugar response than regular white bread. It still contains gluten and similar calories, so it's a better choice rather than a health food. Is sourdough gluten-free? No. Sourdough made from wheat, rye or barley contains gluten. Fermentation breaks down some gluten, but sourdough is not safe for people with coeliac disease. How can I tell if sourdough is real? Real sourdough contains only flour, water and salt, with no added yeast. It has a thick crust, an open, irregular crumb and a mild tang.

# Kozhukattai for Vinayagar Chathurthi: The Kinds, the Meaning, the Making
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/kozhukattai-vinayagar-chathurthi/

Kozhukattai is the steamed rice dumpling made in Tamil homes for Vinayagar Chathurthi, offered to Lord Vinayagar (Ganesha) before the family eats. The best-known kind is sweet, with a coconut and jaggery filling called poornam, but there are also savoury kozhukattai filled with spiced urad dal and pidi kozhukattai pressed by hand. If you'd like to order fresh ones for the festival, our traditional steamed foods page has the details. Book early; the steamer is busy that week. Why kozhukattai for Vinayagar? Vinayagar is often described in stories as being especially fond of modak and kozhukattai. In many tellings, the sweet's shape, a soft outside holding something precious within, is taken as a symbol: an ordinary covering around sweetness, the way wisdom is hidden inside the everyday. Families have their own versions of the meaning. What everyone agrees on is that it's the food of the day, and that the first ones are always for him. The kinds Sweet kozhukattai (poornam kozhukattai). The classic. A thin, soft shell of cooked rice-flour dough around a filling of freshly grated coconut, jaggery and cardamom, often with a little ghee. Shaped like a pleated pouch or a half-moon. Ellu kozhukattai. Filled with roasted sesame seeds and jaggery. Nutty, a little drier, very traditional in some homes. Ulundu kozhukattai (savoury). Filled with a steamed, spiced urad dal mixture, tempered with mustard seeds, curry leaves and green chilli. For the people at the table who find the sweet version too much after the third one. Pidi kozhukattai. "Pidi" means a fistful. The dough is mixed with jaggery and coconut, or with a savoury tempering, and squeezed by hand into a shape that carries the marks of your fingers. No filling, no pleats. Rustic, quick, delicious. Modak. The Maharashtrian cousin, often with a pointed top and many pleats. More on how they differ in kozhukattai or modak. How it's made, the traditional way 1. Rice. Traditionally, raw rice is soaked, dried, ground into fine flour and lightly roasted. Many homes now use store-bought rice flour; the soaked-and-ground version gives a softer, smoother shell. 2. The dough. Water is boiled with a pinch of salt and a few drops of oil, then the flour is stirred in and cooked into a smooth dough. It's kneaded while warm, which is the part that tests your palms. 3. The poornam. Grated coconut and jaggery are cooked together until the mixture thickens and comes together, then finished with cardamom. 4. Shaping. A small ball of dough is pressed into a thin cup, filled, and closed with pleats or folded into a half-moon. Thin is the goal. A thick shell is the most common mistake. 5. Steaming. Ten to twelve minutes in a steamer, until the outside turns faintly glossy and translucent. Eating and keeping Kozhukattai is best warm, within a few hours of steaming. They keep in the fridge for a day; steam them again for two or three minutes before eating and they soften right back. Don't microwave them uncovered, or the shell turns rubbery. Ordering for the festival Everyone wants kozhukattai on the same morning. That's the challenge. If you're ordering from us, book about a week ahead, tell us whether you'd like sweet, savoury, ellu, pidi or a mix, and choose a delivery time early enough for your pooja. We steam in batches through the night so your kozhukattai reaches you on the day, not the day before. Why is kozhukattai made on Vinayagar Chathurthi? Kozhukattai is traditionally considered Lord Vinayagar's favourite food. Families steam it on the morning of the festival and offer it to him before eating it themselves. What are the different types of kozhukattai? The main kinds are sweet kozhukattai with coconut and jaggery, ellu kozhukattai with sesame, savoury ulundu kozhukattai with spiced urad dal, and pidi kozhukattai pressed by hand. How long does kozhukattai stay fresh? Kozhukattai is best eaten the same day. It keeps in the fridge for about a day and should be re-steamed for a few minutes before eating.

# Kozhukattai or Modak? How the Two Dumplings Differ
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/kozhukattai-vs-modak/

Kozhukattai and modak are close cousins: both are rice-flour dumplings filled with coconut and jaggery and steamed for Lord Ganesha. The differences are mostly in shape and region. Maharashtrian ukadiche modak is usually pleated into a tall, pointed teardrop and often richer with ghee. Tamil kozhukattai comes in more shapes, half-moons, pouches and hand-pressed pidi, and has savoury versions too. People sometimes ask me this when they order for Vinayagar Chathurthi, often in families where one side is Tamil and the other grew up in Pune or Mumbai. The honest answer is that both are right. We make both on our traditional steamed foods page. Shape This is the difference you notice first. Modak is shaped into a dome that rises to a point, with many fine pleats running up the sides, sometimes as many as eleven or more. A good modak-maker's pleats are thin and even. In many Maharashtrian homes, the number and neatness of the pleats are a matter of quiet pride. Kozhukattai has more variety. Some homes pleat it into a pouch similar to modak. Many fold it into a half-moon and crimp the edge. Pidi kozhukattai is simply squeezed in the fist. There's less fuss about the exact shape, and more about the filling and the softness of the shell. Filling Both share the classic: grated coconut and jaggery, flavoured with cardamom. Modak fillings are often enriched with ghee, sometimes nutmeg, poppy seeds or dry fruits. There are also fried modak (talniche modak) with a wheat-flour shell, and modern versions with chocolate, mawa and even ice cream. Kozhukattai has its sweet versions (coconut and jaggery, or sesame and jaggery) and a distinct savoury one, ulundu kozhukattai, filled with spiced, steamed urad dal. That savoury branch is one of the biggest differences between the two traditions. Dough Both use rice flour cooked with hot water into a pliable dough. Maharashtrian recipes often add a little ghee or milk to the dough for a softer, richer shell. Tamil recipes typically use water with a few drops of oil. The dough itself is otherwise very similar; much of the difference is technique and family habit. Festival and region Ganesh Chaturthi in Maharashtra is a big public festival, and modak is the signature food, with households and sweet shops making hundreds. In Tamil Nadu, Vinayagar Chathurthi is quieter and more home-centred: a small clay idol, a pooja at home, and kozhukattai as the offering. Karnataka has its own version too, often called kadubu. Which should you make, or order? Make the one your family makes. If your family is both, make both. Vinayagar is not known to be fussy. If you're ordering, tell us the shape your family is used to. A Maharashtrian grandparent will notice if the modak doesn't have its point, and a Tamil grandmother will notice if there's no savoury kozhukattai on the plate. Are modak and kozhukattai the same? They're very similar: both are steamed rice-flour dumplings with a coconut and jaggery filling offered to Ganesha. Modak is the Maharashtrian version, usually pleated into a pointed shape, while kozhukattai is the Tamil version, made in several shapes and also in savoury forms. Which is offered for Vinayagar Chathurthi in Tamil Nadu? In Tamil Nadu, kozhukattai is the traditional offering for Vinayagar Chathurthi, usually both sweet and savoury kinds. Can I order both modak and kozhukattai in Chennai? Yes. The Bake Basket makes both for Vinayagar Chathurthi. Order a few days ahead and mention the shape and fillings your family prefers.

# What Is Vattayappam? Kerala's Soft Steamed Cake for Christmas and Easter
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/what-is-vattayappam/

Vattayappam (also spelt vattappam) is a soft, spongy, steamed rice cake from Kerala, made from a fermented batter of rice and coconut, sweetened with sugar and scented with cardamom, often topped with cashews and raisins. It's traditionally made for Christmas and Easter in Kerala Christian homes, and it tastes like a cross between a fluffy idli and a gentle sponge cake. You can order it fresh from our traditional steamed foods page. What it tastes like If you've never had vattayappam, imagine tearing a piece off a warm, white, round cake. It's springy, almost bouncy, with a fine honeycomb of tiny holes. It smells of cardamom and coconut, faintly of fermentation, like a good appam. It isn't too sweet. It's the kind of thing you eat one wedge of, then come back for a second while pretending to be on your way somewhere else. On Christmas morning, after the midnight mass, it's often eaten with a spicy meat curry, the sweet and spicy together. At Easter, it sits beside the lamb stew. And on an ordinary afternoon, it's lovely on its own with a cup of tea. Why it's fermented The softness comes from fermentation. Rice is soaked and ground with coconut and a little cooked rice or rice flour paste, then left to ferment with yeast, or traditionally with toddy (kallu), the fermented palm sap that once gave Kerala's appams their particular flavour and lift. These days most homes use yeast. During fermentation, the yeast feeds on the sugars in the batter and produces gas, which forms all those tiny bubbles. When the batter is steamed, the bubbles expand and set, and you get that light, springy crumb. Rush the ferment, and the vattayappam is flat and heavy. Over-ferment, and it's sour. How it's made 1. Soak raw rice for several hours. 2. Grind it with freshly grated coconut into a smooth batter, adding a small amount of cooked rice for softness. 3. Ferment with yeast and sugar for several hours, or overnight, depending on the weather. In Chennai's warmth, it ferments fast. In the cooler months, it takes longer. 4. Flavour with crushed cardamom and sugar. 5. Pour into a greased round plate and top with cashews and raisins, often fried lightly in ghee. 6. Steam for about 20 to 25 minutes until it's risen, set and springs back when pressed. 7. Cool a little before cutting, so the wedges come out clean. Vattayappam, appam and kinnathappam They're relatives. Appam (palappam) uses a similar fermented rice and coconut batter, but it's cooked in a curved pan to make a lacy, crisp-edged pancake with a soft centre. Vattayappam is the same family, steamed thick into a cake. Kinnathappam, from Malabar, is a different steamed sweet, smoother and denser, made with rice flour and coconut milk, set and sliced. Christmas and Easter In many Kerala Christian homes, Christmas preparations include the plum cake, the wine (or grape juice) set to ferment weeks earlier, the meat curry, and vattayappam made on Christmas Eve or early on Christmas morning. At Easter, after the long Lenten fast, vattayappam returns to the table. For families living in Chennai, away from the tharavad and the grandmothers who made it, it's often the dish that's most missed. That's the reason we make it. Our Christmas plum cake sits beside it on the festive menu. Keeping it Vattayappam is best on the day it's steamed. It keeps in a covered container at room temperature for a day in cool weather, and in the fridge for two. Steam slices for a few minutes to soften them again. What is vattayappam made of? Vattayappam is made from rice and coconut ground into a batter, fermented with yeast (traditionally toddy), sweetened with sugar and flavoured with cardamom, then steamed. It's often topped with cashews and raisins. When is vattayappam eaten? Vattayappam is traditionally made for Christmas and Easter in Kerala Christian homes, but many families enjoy it year-round with tea or with curries. What's the difference between appam and vattayappam? Both use a fermented rice and coconut batter. Appam is cooked in a curved pan into a thin, lacy pancake, while vattayappam is steamed into a thick, soft, sweet cake.

# Ela Ada: The Banana-Leaf Sweet That Tastes Like Onam
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/ela-ada-onam/

Ela ada (also written elayada or ila ada) is a Kerala sweet made by spreading a thin layer of rice-flour dough on a piece of banana leaf, filling it with coconut and jaggery, folding it closed and steaming it. "Ela" means leaf and "ada" is the rice parcel. The leaf gives it a faint, green, almost smoky fragrance that nothing else can. It's made all year as a tea-time snack, and with special affection at Onam. If you're in Chennai and missing it, our traditional steamed foods include ela ada made the old way. The moment you open it That's what people remember. You unfold the leaf, still warm, and the steam carries the smell of jaggery, coconut and wilted banana leaf all at once. The ada itself is soft and slightly sticky, almost translucent at the edges, and the leaf leaves a faint imprint of its veins on the rice. The filling has melted into a dark, sweet, coconut-heavy layer that's best eaten with your fingers, carefully, because it's hot. What goes into it The dough. Rice flour (traditionally, roasted rice flour) mixed with hot water and a pinch of salt into a soft, spreadable dough. Some homes add a little coconut oil or ghee. The filling. Freshly grated coconut cooked with jaggery until thick and glossy, flavoured with cardamom. Some families add ripe banana, especially the Kerala nendran banana. Others add jackfruit when it's in season, which makes chakka ada, one of the most loved variations. The leaf. Fresh banana leaf, cut into rectangles and softened by passing it briefly over a flame or dipping it in hot water, so it folds without tearing. How it's made 1. Wipe the banana leaf pieces clean and soften them. 2. Spread a thin layer of dough on one half of the leaf with wet fingers. 3. Spoon the filling along the centre. 4. Fold the leaf over, press the edges gently to seal the dough. 5. Steam for about 10 to 15 minutes, until the dough turns slightly translucent. 6. Let it rest for a few minutes before unwrapping. The ada sets a little as it cools. The hard part is the thinness. Too thick and it's stodgy. Too thin and it tears. There's a reason grandmothers made it look easy. Ela ada and Onam Onam is Kerala's harvest festival, and the sadhya, the great vegetarian feast on a banana leaf, is its centre. Ela ada isn't usually part of the sadhya itself, but it's one of the sweets that appears around the festival, made in homes in the days before and after, offered to visitors with tea. Ada pradhaman, the payasam made with rice ada, is the sadhya's star dessert, and it shares a name and a family resemblance. For Malayali families in Chennai, Onam often means a sadhya ordered from a caterer, a pookalam made in a small flat entrance, and a longing for the snacks that a grandmother would have made without being asked. That's where ela ada comes in. Variations worth knowing - Chakka ada: with jackfruit, during jackfruit season - Banana ada: with ripe nendran banana mashed into the filling - Wheat ada: using wheat flour instead of rice, a little more chewy - Ari ada: the plain rice version, often for ada pradhaman Keeping it Ela ada is best eaten warm, on the day. In the fridge it keeps for a day, wrapped in its leaf. Steam it again for five minutes to bring back the softness. What is ela ada? Ela ada is a Kerala snack made by spreading rice-flour dough on banana leaf, filling it with coconut and jaggery, folding it and steaming it. The leaf gives it a distinctive fragrance. Is ela ada healthy? Ela ada is steamed, not fried, and made with rice, coconut and jaggery, which makes it a lighter sweet than many fried snacks. It still contains sugar from the jaggery, so it's a treat. Can I order ela ada in Chennai? Yes. The Bake Basket makes ela ada to order in Chennai, steamed in banana leaf. Order a day or two ahead, and earlier around Onam.

# Why Kerala Plum Cake Fruit Soaks for Weeks
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/kerala-plum-cake-soaking-fruit/

Dried fruit for a Kerala plum cake is soaked for weeks (sometimes months) so it plumps up, softens, and absorbs flavour, which keeps the finished cake moist and lets the fruit and spice blend into one deep taste. The soaking liquid is traditionally rum or brandy, which also helps the cake keep; juice works for an alcohol-free cake that's eaten sooner. The very dark colour comes from caramelised sugar, not from chocolate. My fruit jar goes on the shelf long before anyone in the house is thinking about Christmas. You can book yours on our Christmas plum cake page. What goes into the jar Black raisins, golden raisins, chopped dates, dried figs or apricots, candied orange peel, tutti-frutti, glazed cherries, cashews. Every family has its own mix and its own strong opinions. Some swear by adding ginger preserve; others insist on prunes. The fruit is chopped, layered into a clean glass jar, and covered with the soaking liquid. Then it's sealed and left somewhere cool and dark, and stirred or shaken now and then. What the soaking does It softens the fruit. Dried fruit is tough and chewy. Weeks of soaking turn it plump and almost jammy. It stops the fruit drying the cake. Dry fruit pulls moisture out of the batter as the cake bakes. Fruit that's already full of liquid gives moisture back instead, which is why a good plum cake stays moist for weeks. It blends the flavours. Over time, the fruits taste less like separate ingredients and more like one thing, rich and dark and slightly boozy. It helps the cake keep. Alcohol is a preservative. A rum-soaked plum cake, well wrapped, keeps far longer than most cakes. Alcohol or not? Rum and brandy are the traditional choices in Kerala, and they give a deeper, warmer flavour. The alcohol largely bakes off from the cake itself, but some remains, especially if the cake is "fed" with a little more after baking. For families who don't drink, or who are serving children, the fruit can be soaked in orange juice, grape juice or strong black tea. The cake tastes lighter and fruitier, and it doesn't keep as long, so it's best within a week or two. The caramel Kerala plum cake is darker than most fruit cakes, and the secret isn't cocoa. It's caramel: sugar cooked in a pan until it turns very dark brown, almost burnt, then thinned with hot water. This syrup goes into the batter and gives the cake its deep colour and a faint bitterness that balances all the sweet fruit. Getting the caramel right is the difference between a good plum cake and a great one. Too pale, and the cake looks anaemic. Too dark, and it tastes burnt. It's done by eye and smell. The spices Cinnamon, clove, nutmeg, and sometimes a little dry ginger and cardamom. Ground fresh if possible. When the cake is baking, the whole house smells like December. How long does it keep? Plum cake Keeps for ------ Rum or brandy soaked, well wrapped, cool place 3 to 4 weeks, sometimes longer Rum or brandy soaked, in the fridge Up to 2 months Alcohol-free (juice soaked) About 1 to 2 weeks in a cool place, longer in the fridge Many people think a plum cake tastes best a few days after baking, once the flavours have settled. Wrap it in butter paper and then in foil or a cloth, and keep it in a tin. Why is it called "plum" cake when there are no plums? In old English, "plum" was used for raisins and dried fruit in general. That's why there's a plum pudding with no plums in it. The name came to India with the British, and stuck. Why do you soak fruit for plum cake? Soaking plumps and softens the dried fruit, keeps the cake moist by stopping the fruit pulling moisture from the batter, blends the flavours, and, if alcohol is used, helps the cake keep longer. How long should fruit be soaked for plum cake? Many Kerala bakers soak fruit for several weeks, and some for months. Even a few days of soaking improves the cake, but longer soaking gives a deeper flavour. Can plum cake be made without alcohol? Yes. Fruit can be soaked in orange juice, grape juice or tea instead. Alcohol-free plum cake tastes lighter and should be eaten within about one to two weeks.

---

# Christmas Food in Chennai's Kerala and Tamil Christian Homes
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/christmas-food-chennai-homes/

Christmas in Kerala and Tamil Christian homes is defined as much by food as by the star on the balcony. In Kerala homes: plum cake, appam with stew or a spicy meat curry, vattayappam, rose cookies (achappam) and kuzhalappam, and homemade wine. In Tamil Christian homes: plum cake, biryani for the Christmas lunch, kalkal (kulkuls), rose cookies and sweets shared with neighbours. In Chennai, the two traditions often sit on the same table. The weeks before Christmas food starts early. The fruit for the plum cake goes into its jar in October or November. Grapes are crushed for homemade wine weeks ahead. In the last fortnight, the kitchen turns into a factory of fried snacks: achappam, kuzhalappam and kalkal are made in quantities that seem absurd, because they're meant to be given away. The tradition of sharing is central. Plates of sweets go to Hindu and Muslim neighbours, who will send plates back at Deepavali and Eid. In many Chennai apartment blocks, those plates are how people who barely speak the rest of the year end up knowing each other's children's names. The Kerala table Appam and stew. Lacy-edged, soft-centred appam with a mild, creamy stew of chicken, mutton or vegetables cooked in coconut milk with whole spices. Christmas breakfast in many homes. Vattayappam. The steamed cousin of appam, sweet and soft, often eaten with the meat curry. More in what is vattayappam. Duck roast, beef fry, meen moilee. The heavy hitters for lunch, depending on the family and the region. Plum cake. Dark, rich, cut into thick slices and offered to every visitor. Achappam and kuzhalappam. Achappam (rose cookies) are crisp, lacy flowers made with a special iron mould dipped in batter and fried. Kuzhalappam are crunchy rolled tubes. Both are made in big batches and stored in tins. Homemade wine. Grape wine made at home, though many families now make a non-alcoholic grape juice version. The Tamil Christian table Biryani. In many Tamil Christian homes in and around Chennai, Christmas lunch means biryani, often mutton, with raita and a brinjal curry. Kalkal (kulkuls). Small curled dough pieces, fried and coated in sugar. Children traditionally help shape them on the back of a fork. Rose cookies. Shared with Kerala homes. Plum cake. Bought from a favourite bakery or made at home. Sweets for neighbours. Plates of kalkal, rose cookies, cake and murukku, carried door to door. When you're far from home For many families who've moved to Chennai from Kerala or the southern districts, Christmas is the time they miss home most. Grandmothers who made achappam are far away, or gone. The jar of fruit isn't on the shelf. The working week runs right up to the 24th. It's completely fine to order some of it. A plum cake and vattayappam from someone who makes them carefully, the same way, can bring the house back to how it used to smell. Our gift hampers include Christmas baskets with plum cake, vattayappam and cookies, delivered in a real basket to take to church friends, neighbours or your own parents. A simple Christmas plan When What ------ Early November Book plum cake and Christmas baskets Mid December Order cookie tins and vattayappam for Christmas Eve 24 December Collect or receive deliveries; set aside a plate for neighbours 25 December morning Appam and stew, vattayappam 25 December lunch Biryani or duck roast, depending on the family The week after Plum cake with tea, every afternoon until it's gone What is the traditional Christmas food in Kerala? Traditional Kerala Christmas food includes plum cake, appam with stew, vattayappam, duck roast or beef fry, achappam (rose cookies), kuzhalappam and homemade wine. What do Tamil Christians eat at Christmas? Many Tamil Christian families have biryani for Christmas lunch, along with plum cake, kalkal, rose cookies and sweets shared with neighbours. When should I order Christmas plum cake in Chennai? Book Christmas plum cake by early to mid November. Bakers make limited batches, and December fills up quickly.

# Puttu, Idiyappam and Appam: A Guide to Kerala's Steamed Breakfasts
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/puttu-idiyappam-appam-guide/

Puttu is steamed rice flour layered with grated coconut in a tall cylinder. Idiyappam (string hoppers, called sevai in parts of Tamil Nadu) is rice dough pressed into fine noodles and steamed into soft nests. Appam is a fermented rice and coconut batter cooked in a curved pan into a lacy pancake with a soft middle. All three are rice-based, and all three are breakfast staples in Kerala and in many Tamil homes. You'll find them on our traditional steamed foods page. Puttu How it's made. Rice flour is moistened with salted water until it's damp and crumbly, like wet sand, but not a dough. It's layered into a puttu kutti (a steaming cylinder) with grated coconut between the layers, and steamed for a few minutes. It slides out as a log striped white with coconut. Texture. Soft, crumbly, light. It falls apart when you press it with your fingers, which is exactly how you're meant to eat it. Eat it with. Kadala curry (black chickpea curry) is the classic. Also banana and sugar, ripe pappadam crushed over it, or fish curry. In some homes, a spoonful of ghee and sugar for children. Variations. Ragi puttu, wheat puttu, corn puttu, and chiratta puttu, steamed in a coconut shell. Idiyappam How it's made. Rice flour is cooked with hot water into a soft dough, then pressed through a mould (a sevai nazhi) into thin noodles onto steaming plates, in small nests. Steamed for about ten minutes. Texture. Soft, delicate, light. Each strand separate, the whole nest gently springy. Eat it with. Kerala stew, egg curry, chicken curry, kurma. Sweet coconut milk with sugar and cardamom. Grated coconut and sugar for a simple breakfast. In Tamil Nadu. It's often called sevai and turned into lemon sevai, coconut sevai or tamarind sevai, tossed with tempering. Appam How it's made. Rice is ground with coconut and fermented with yeast, or traditionally with toddy, overnight. The batter is poured into a hot appachatti (a small, deep, curved pan) and swirled, so it spreads thin up the sides and pools in the centre. Covered and cooked without flipping. Texture. Crisp, lacy, golden edges; thick, soft, spongy centre. The contrast is the whole point. Eat it with. Stew, above all. Also egg roast, chicken curry, or coconut milk with sugar. Its relatives. Vattayappam is a steamed, sweet, thick cake from a similar batter; we explain it in what is vattayappam. Kallappam is a flatter, toddy-fermented version. Idli, for completeness The Tamil classic needs no introduction in Chennai, but it fits here. Fermented rice and urad dal batter, steamed in moulds. Kanchipuram idli adds pepper, cumin, ginger and ghee. Rava idli uses semolina and curd and needs no fermentation. Millet idlis are increasingly popular for everyday breakfasts. Side by side Puttu Idiyappam Appam Idli --------------- Base Rice flour (or ragi, wheat) Rice flour Fermented rice and coconut Fermented rice and urad dal Cooking Steamed in a cylinder Pressed and steamed Pan-cooked, covered Steamed in moulds Fermented? No No Yes Yes Texture Crumbly, soft Fine, springy strands Lacy edge, soft centre Soft, spongy Classic pairing Kadala curry Stew, coconut milk Stew Sambar, chutney Ordering them in Chennai Appam is best eaten within minutes of leaving the pan, so it's the hardest to deliver well. Puttu and idiyappam travel well if they're steamed close to delivery time and kept covered; a quick re-steam at home brings them back to fresh. Order them for a Sunday breakfast, a family visit or a lunch for someone recovering at home; they're gentle and easy to digest. What is the difference between puttu and idiyappam? Puttu is crumbly steamed rice flour layered with coconut in a cylinder, while idiyappam is rice dough pressed into fine noodles and steamed into soft nests. Both are rice-based breakfasts from Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Is idiyappam the same as sevai? Yes, they're essentially the same: steamed rice noodles. In Tamil Nadu, sevai is often tossed with lemon, coconut or tamarind seasoning after steaming. Which is healthier, puttu or appam? Both are made from rice and coconut. Puttu is steamed with no oil, while appam uses a little oil in the pan and is fermented. Ragi or wheat puttu adds extra fibre.

# A Deepavali Basket That Isn't Just Sweets
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/deepavali-gift-basket-ideas/

The best Deepavali baskets balance sweet with savoury and traditional with something a little new: a tin of nankhatai or coconut cookies, a box of brownies, a small cake or loaf, something savoury like jeera cookies or cheese straws, and a handwritten note. It stands out because every house already gets six boxes of the same mithai. Order at least a week ahead, and three to four weeks for office quantities. You can see what goes into ours on the gift hampers page. The sweet-box problem By Deepavali evening, most Chennai kitchens have a counter stacked with boxes: Mysore pak, kaju katli, laddoos, a bit of everything. They're lovely. They're also, by the fourth box, a little indistinguishable. Half end up re-gifted. Some end up in the fridge until January. A basket that looks and tastes different gets noticed. It's opened first, not last. What to put in A good basket has a mix, roughly in these parts: Something traditional. Nankhatai, coconut cookies, cashew cookies, or a few pieces of homemade mithai. It's Deepavali; tradition matters. Something rich. A box of fudgy brownies or a small chocolate cake. The children of the house will find this first. Something savoury. Jeera cookies, cheese straws, savoury biscuits. Essential for the uncle who "doesn't eat sweets" and for the evening after three days of sugar. Something for the morning after. A loaf of brioche, banana bread or a fruit cake for breakfast. Something lighter. A few millet or jaggery bakes for anyone watching sugar. More thoughtful than it sounds. A personal note. Handwritten, with the family's name. By recipient Your parents or in-laws. Traditional cookies, a fruit cake, millet bakes if anyone watches sugar, and something nostalgic like coconut buns. Neighbours. Smaller baskets with cookies and brownies. In apartment blocks, consistency matters more than size; everyone on the floor should get the same. Your domestic help, security and drivers. A generous, practical basket: a cake, cookies and savoury snacks for their whole family. Often more appreciated than anything else you give. Colleagues and your team. Individual boxes, or one large basket for the office pantry. Read corporate Deepavali gifting for more. Clients. A premium basket with your card, delivered to their home rather than the office, because that's where Deepavali happens. A few rules - Label everything, especially anything with nuts or egg. - Avoid cream-based items; baskets sit around for a day or two. - Choose bakes that keep for at least three or four days. - Don't overfill; a basket that looks abundant but tidy is better than one that's crammed. - Use a real basket if you can. People keep them, and reuse them, and remember who gave them. When to order What Order by ------ A few family baskets 7 to 10 days before Deepavali 10 to 30 baskets (neighbours, staff) 2 weeks before Office and client quantities 3 to 4 weeks before What should I put in a Deepavali gift basket? Mix traditional cookies or sweets, something rich like brownies, something savoury, a breakfast bake such as fruit cake or brioche, and a handwritten note. Add millet or jaggery bakes for anyone watching sugar. When should I order Deepavali hampers in Chennai? Order family hampers at least a week ahead, and corporate or bulk hampers three to four weeks before Deepavali. How long do Deepavali hamper items last? Cookies and brownies usually last four to seven days, fruit cakes about a week or more. Avoid cream-based items in gift baskets.

# Chennai's Festival Food Calendar, From Pongal to Christmas
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/chennai-festival-food-calendar/

Chennai's year runs on festival food. January brings sweet pongal; spring brings Ramzan's sharing plates, Tamil New Year and Vishu; August and September bring kozhukattai for Vinayagar Chathurthi and the Onam sadhya; Navaratri brings sundal; Deepavali brings sweets and gift baskets; December brings plum cake and vattayappam. Here's the year, month by month, with what to eat and when to order. Festival dates move with the lunar and solar calendars, so always check the year's exact date. Our traditional steamed foods and gift hampers follow this calendar. January: Pongal Pongal, the Tamil harvest festival, runs over four days in mid-January: Bhogi, Thai Pongal, Mattu Pongal and Kaanum Pongal. The food is the festival's name: pongal, rice cooked in a new pot until it boils over, a sign of abundance. Sakkarai pongal (sweet, with jaggery, ghee, cashews and cardamom) and ven pongal (savoury, with pepper and cumin) both appear, along with sugarcane, turmeric plants and a great deal of goodwill. Order ahead: baskets for family and colleagues a week before. February: Valentine's Day Not a traditional festival, but a busy date for small cakes, bento cakes and cupcake boxes. Order ahead: two or three days; earlier if it falls on a weekend. Ramzan and Eid (dates shift each year) Through Ramzan, evenings in Chennai's Muslim neighbourhoods smell of nombu kanji, the rice porridge distributed at mosques for iftar. Samosas, dates, fruit and sharing plates go to neighbours. Eid ul-Fitr brings biryani, sheer khurma and plates of sweets sent across the street, often to Hindu and Christian neighbours, who send plates back at their own festivals. Order ahead: sharing boxes and Eid baskets a week ahead. March or April: Easter In Kerala and Tamil Christian homes, Easter ends the Lenten fast. Appam and stew return to breakfast, along with vattayappam, and lamb or chicken for lunch. Order ahead: vattayappam two or three days before. April: Tamil New Year and Vishu Tamil New Year (Puthandu), usually on 14 April, is marked with a meal that includes mango pachadi, a dish that's sweet, sour, bitter and spicy at once, a reminder that a year holds all of them. Kerala's Vishu falls around the same day, with the Vishukkani arrangement at dawn and a festive sadhya. May: Mother's Day A gentle, busy day for cakes, cupcake bouquets and baskets for mothers and grandmothers. June: back to school Lunchbox bakes and class birthday cupcakes. See lunchbox bakes kids will eat. August or September: Vinayagar Chathurthi Clay Vinayagar idols arrive home, and kitchens fill with steam. Sweet and savoury kozhukattai, modak, sundal and fruit are offered before anyone eats. See kozhukattai for Vinayagar Chathurthi. Order ahead: at least a week before. August or September: Onam The Malayali harvest festival, ten days long, ending in Thiruvonam. The sadhya, two dozen or more dishes on a banana leaf, is the centre, with payasams to finish. Ela ada and banana chips are close to hand. See ela ada. Order ahead: sadhyas from caterers two weeks before; snacks and ada a few days before. September or October: Navaratri Nine nights of golu, the stepped display of dolls, and visiting. Every evening a different sundal: chickpea, green gram, peanut, black-eyed bean. Small sweets and return gifts (thamboolam) for women and girls who visit. Order ahead: thamboolam packs and small sweet boxes a week before the first evening. October or November: Deepavali The biggest gifting week of the year. Sweets, savouries, new clothes, early-morning oil baths, and baskets carried to family, neighbours and colleagues. See a Deepavali basket that isn't just sweets. Order ahead: family baskets a week before; corporate orders three to four weeks before. December: Christmas and New Year Plum cake, vattayappam, rose cookies, kalkal, appam and stew, biryani for lunch, and stars on balconies across the city. New Year's Eve brings parties and late cake orders. See Christmas food in Chennai homes. Order ahead: plum cake by early to mid November. What are the main festival foods in Chennai? Key festival foods include sweet and savoury pongal for Pongal, kozhukattai for Vinayagar Chathurthi, sundal for Navaratri, sweets and savouries for Deepavali, sheer khurma and biryani for Eid, ela ada and payasam for Onam, and plum cake and vattayappam for Christmas. When should I order festival sweets in Chennai? For most festivals, order at least a week ahead. For Deepavali corporate gifting and Christmas plum cakes, book three to six weeks ahead. What is eaten on Tamil New Year? Tamil New Year meals often include mango pachadi, which combines sweet, sour, bitter and spicy tastes, along with vadai, payasam and a festive vegetarian meal.

---

# What to Send Someone in Hospital (Food That Actually Helps)
URL: https://thebakebasket.com/blog/what-to-send-someone-in-hospital/

Before you send food to someone in hospital, ask the family what the patient is allowed to eat; many patients are on restricted diets. If they can eat normally, send small amounts of gentle, mild food: soft bread, plain cake, idiyappam, rusks, fruit. Often the most useful thing is food for the family sitting by the bed, who are surviving on canteen coffee. That last point is the one people forget. We build care baskets around it. Check first Hospitals are not the place for surprises. A patient might be fasting before a procedure, on a diabetic diet, a low-salt diet, a soft diet, or nothing by mouth at all. Some hospitals don't allow outside food in certain wards. Message a family member: "Is there anything he can eat? Would the family like some food?" It's a kind question, and it saves wasted food and awkward moments. If the patient can eat normally Choose food that's: - Gentle. Mild, not spicy, not oily. - Small. A few pieces, not a 1 kg cake. Appetite is usually low. - Easy to eat in bed. No crumbs everywhere, no sauces, no knives. - Not too sweet. Very sweet food can be unappealing when someone's unwell. - Easy to store. Hospital rooms rarely have a fridge. Good choices: soft milk bread or rusks, a plain tea cake or banana bread, idiyappam with mild coconut milk, soft idlis, fresh fruit that's easy to eat (bananas, oranges, grapes), plain biscuits, homemade kanji if you know they'll like it. Avoid: cream cakes, heavily spiced food, fried snacks, strong-smelling food (other patients share the room), and anything that needs reheating. For someone recovering at home This is where food really helps. Someone home after surgery or a long illness often can't cook, and their family is exhausted. Useful things: - Soft bread and a loaf of whole-wheat or multigrain for breakfasts - Idiyappam, puttu or idli batter for easy meals - A mild cake or banana bread for visitors - Soups or kanji, if you're close enough to bring them warm - Fruit Send it in small quantities, more than once, rather than everything in one day. For the family by the bed When someone's in hospital, the people around them stop eating properly. They live on canteen samosas, tea and whatever's in the vending machine. A basket for them, quietly delivered, is often more appreciated than anything for the patient. - Sandwiches or savoury buns - Brownies or cookies for energy - Muffins - Fruit - A flask of something warm, if you can The note matters most A handwritten note that says "Thinking of you all, no need to reply" takes the pressure off. People in hospital rooms get too many messages to answer. Let them off the hook. What not to send - Flowers to ICUs and many wards; check, because many hospitals no longer allow them - Large quantities that will go to waste - Anything with alcohol - Food that needs a fridge, unless you know there is one What food can I take to someone in hospital? First check with the family what the patient is allowed to eat. If they can eat normally, take small amounts of gentle food like soft bread, plain cake, idiyappam, rusks or easy-to-eat fruit. What is a good get-well gift for someone recovering at home? Easy, gentle food in small amounts, such as soft breads, mild cakes, idiyappam or idli, along with fruit. A basket for the family helps too, as they often have no time to cook. Can I send cake to a hospital patient? A small, plain cake such as banana bread or tea cake can be fine if the patient's diet allows it. Avoid cream cakes, which need refrigeration and are often too rich.
